subject: psychiatry
title: Alcoholic Hallucinosis and Relapse Prevention Pharmacotherapy

steps.tx: **Alcoholic hallucinosis** is a distinct psychiatric syndrome developing within 12 to 24 hours following the cessation or reduction of heavy alcohol intake. Sufferers experience vivid, threatening auditory hallucinations, typically comprising persecutory voices speaking in the third person, while maintaining a completely clear sensorium and intact orientation.
steps.say: Alcoholic hallucinosis presents within twenty-four hours of drinking cessation with threatening auditory hallucinations, while orientation and consciousness remain completely clear.

left.title: Alcoholic Hallucinosis
points: Absence of autonomic storm or hyperthermia

steps.tx: **Clinical course of alcoholic hallucinosis** is typically self-limiting, resolving spontaneously within 48 hours to several weeks upon sustained alcohol abstinence. A small subset of chronic patients develops a persistent hallucinatory state resembling paranoid schizophrenia, termed chronic alcoholic hallucinosis, requiring long-term second-generation antipsychotic maintenance.
steps.say: Most hallucinosis episodes resolve within several days with abstinence and antipsychotics. A small fraction develops a chronic schizophrenia-like syndrome.

nodes.label: Abrupt cessation of chronic heavy alcohol consumption
Emergence of vivid auditory hallucinations within 24 hours
Full symptomatic resolution in >90% within one to two weeks

steps.tx: **Disulfiram pharmacodynamics** establish it as an irreversible inhibitor of aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), the liver enzyme responsible for metabolizing toxic acetaldehyde into harmless acetate. When alcohol is ingested concurrently, acetaldehyde accumulates up to ten-fold in circulating plasma, precipitating an excruciatingly unpleasant physiological reaction.
steps.say: Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing toxic acetaldehyde to surge ten-fold if alcohol is consumed, triggering a severe physiological reaction.

nodes.label: Ethanol converted to acetaldehyde via alcohol dehydrogenase
Disulfiram irreversibly blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase enzyme
Toxic accumulation of circulating blood acetaldehyde
Severe flushing, tachycardia, hypotension, nausea, & panic

steps.tx: **Disulfiram-ethanol reaction** develops within 10 to 15 minutes of alcohol ingestion, presenting with intense facial flushing, throbbing headache, diaphoresis, nausea, intractable vomiting, chest pain, and profound hypotension. In severe cases, the reaction causes cardiovascular collapse, myocardial infarction, and death, mandating strict informed patient consent.
steps.say: The disulfiram-ethanol reaction causes facial flushing, vomiting, tachycardia, chest pain, and severe hypotension, requiring strict consent before prescription.

vis.alt: Hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase pathways and neurochemical dependence mechanisms
vis.caption: Hepatic alcohol dehydrogenase pathways and neurochemical dependence mechanisms.

steps.tx: **Clinical precautions with disulfiram** require absolute abstinence from alcohol for at least 12 hours before therapy initiation, warning patients to avoid hidden alcohol in cough syrups, cooking sauces, aftershaves, and mouthwashes. Because enzyme resynthesis takes up to two weeks, the reaction can occur for 14 days after stopping disulfiram.
steps.say: Patients must be abstinent for twelve hours before starting disulfiram. The reaction can occur for up to two weeks after stopping due to slow enzyme resynthesis.

left.title: Hidden Ethanol Sources
points: Cooking vinegars, desserts, and flambe dishes

right.title: Absolute Contraindications
points: Severe coronary artery disease & heart failure
Active hepatic cirrhosis or severe dysfunction
Psychotic disorders and severe cognitive decline

steps.tx: **Naltrexone in alcohol dependence** operates as a competitive antagonist at mu-opioid receptors, blocking endogenous endorphin release elicited by alcohol consumption. By severing the neurochemical reward associated with drinking, naltrexone significantly diminishes alcohol craving and prevents a slip from escalating into a full relapse.
steps.say: Naltrexone blocks mu-opioid receptors to extinguish alcohol-induced euphoria and cravings. It is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and opioid therapy.

vis.title: Naltrexone Pharmacology Summary
rows: 50 mg once daily orally (or depot monthly)
Allows patients to stop after one or two drinks
Contraindicated in acute hepatitis or liver failure

steps.tx: **Acamprosate calcium** is a synthetic taurine analogue that restores balance between central GABAergic inhibition and NMDA glutamatergic excitation disrupted by chronic alcohol consumption. Because acamprosate is cleared entirely by renal excretion without undergoing hepatic metabolism, it serves as the preferred anticraving medication in cirrhotic liver disease.
steps.say: Acamprosate modulates NMDA and GABA transmission to sustain abstinence. Because it is renally excreted, it is safe in patients with hepatic disease.

left.title: Acamprosate Strengths
points: Proven efficacy in maintaining total abstinence
Completely safe in hepatic cirrhosis & hepatitis
No drug interactions with CYP450 enzymes

right.title: Clinical Limitations
points: Requires taking two tablets three times daily
Frequent transient diarrhea in initial weeks
Ineffective if active heavy drinking continues

steps.tx: **Comparison of anticraving medications** guides personalized psychiatric selection: naltrexone is optimal for actively drinking patients aiming to reduce heavy consumption, whereas acamprosate is optimal for motivated patients pursuing complete abstinence, especially those with hepatic impairment or cirrhosis where naltrexone is strictly contraindicated.
steps.say: Naltrexone suits individuals seeking to reduce binge drinking. Acamprosate is preferred for motivated abstinence, particularly in patients with liver disease.

vis.title: Pharmacotherapy Selection Matrix
rows: Acute liver failure; concurrent opioid use
